claims.text: Set the bench at 30-45 degrees; steeper shifts work to the shoulders. In EMG data the upper chest peaked at 30 degrees, and above 45 degrees front-shoulder activity was significantly higher and chest performance lower.

quotes.text: Set the bench to an incline angle of 30 to 45 degrees. A steeper angle shifts more focus to the shoulders, while a lower angle targets the chest more effectively.
The results showed that the maximal EMG activity for PMUP occurred at a bench inclination of 30°.
Inclinations greater than 45° produce significantly higher activation of the anterior deltoid and decrease the muscular performance of the pectoralis major.

claims.text: While pressing up, the upper (clavicular) chest was more active on a 45-degree incline barbell bench than on the flat bench or chest-press machine; while lowering, the flat bench was higher.

quotes.text: During the concentric phase, [d effect size: 2.78/7.80] clavicular head was more excited in IBP and less excited in CP (d: -9.69/-4.39) compared to all other exercises.
Muscle excitation during the eccentric phase followed a similar pattern, with the exception of the greater (d: 3.89/11.32) excitation in the clavicular head in BP compared to all other exercises.

claims.text: Head, shoulders and hips stay firmly on the bench; feet flat on the floor or footrests.

quotes.text: Lie back on the incline bench with your feet flat on the ground or footrests for stability. Position your head, shoulders, and hips firmly against the bench.

claims.text: Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width, palms forward, wrists straight.

quotes.text: Grasp the barbell with a slightly wider-than-shoulder-width grip. Your palms should face forward, and your wrists should remain straight.

claims.text: Start with the bar unracked and held on straight arms above the shoulders.

quotes.text: Sitting on an inclined bench, unrack a barbell and hold it on straight arms above your shoulders.

claims.text: A way out: use a spotter for the lift-off and for heavier sets, and safety catches.

quotes.text: With the help of a spotter, unrack the barbell and hold it directly above your chest with arms fully extended.
Use a spotter, especially for barbell lifts.
use safety catches if needed.

claims.text: Lower the bar slowly to the upper chest with the elbows about 45-75 degrees from the torso.

quotes.text: Slowly lower the barbell toward your upper chest, maintaining control and keeping your elbows at a 45-75 degree angle relative to your torso.
Unrack the bar and lower it to the upper chest.

claims.text: Common faults: an incline set too steep, elbows flared out (shoulder strain), and bouncing the bar off the chest.

quotes.text: Setting the incline too steep, which shifts focus away from the chest.
Allowing the elbows to flare out excessively, increasing shoulder strain.
Using momentum or bouncing the barbell off your chest.

claims.text: Keep a neutral spine and do not over-arch the low back; excessive arching is named as an injury risk.

quotes.text: Maintain a neutral spine and avoid arching your back excessively.
Shoulder strain from flared elbows, lower back arching excessively, wrist strain from poor grip angle

claims.text: Triceps activity was similar at every bench angle from flat to 60 degrees.

quotes.text: TB showed similar EMG activities at all bench inclinations.

claims.text: The lower chest still works at 30 degrees (about 87% of maximal voluntary activation, vs about 100% flat), and drops at 45 degrees.

quotes.text: The sEMG of lower pectoralis was greater during -15° (100.4 ± 5.7% MVIC), 30° (86.6 ± 4.8% MVIC) and horizontal (100.1 ± 5.2% MVIC) bench conditions compared to the 45° (71.9 ± 4.5% MVIC)

claims.text: Stop if you feel pain in the shoulders or chest, and progress to heavier weights gradually.

quotes.text: Stop immediately if you feel pain or discomfort in your shoulders or chest.
Progress gradually to heavier weights to avoid injury.

claims.text: Add load in small steps: ACSM recommends a 2-10% increase once the current load can be done for one to two reps over the target.

quotes.text: it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number

claims.text: ACSM recommends a moderate speed for strength work: 1-2 seconds up and 1-2 seconds down.

quotes.text: using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: Barbells pressing on the neck have killed weightlifters by traumatic asphyxia; the incline touch point (upper chest) is the one closest to the neck.

quotes.text: an unrecognized source of accidental asphyxia--compression of the neck by barbells

There have been at least 11 similar deaths reported to the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) and cataloged in the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System between 1999 and 2002.

claims.text: Across US emergency-department weight-training injuries, the most common mechanism was weights dropping on the person, and 90% involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

extrinsic risk factors, namely, that of improper attention to exercise technique

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; bench angle, the upper-chest touch point and the low-back arch all read in the sagittal plane (c1, c7, c9).
plate.equipment: Incline bench with its own rack, back pad at 30 degrees (inside the 30-45 range of c1, and the angle where upper-chest EMG peaked, c1); barbell; feet flat (c3). Safety catches are drawn on the rack (c6).
plate.start: On the incline, head, shoulders and hips on the pad, feet flat (c3); bar on straight arms above the shoulders (c5).
plate.end: Bar touching the upper chest (c7), elbows about 45-75 degrees from the torso (c7), back and hips still on the pad (c3, c9).

checkpoints.label: Bench at 30°
checkpoints.what: Back pad at about 30 degrees, not steeper than 45.

checkpoints.label: To upper chest
checkpoints.what: Bar comes down under control to the top of the chest, not the neck.

checkpoints.label: Back on pad
checkpoints.what: Head, shoulders and hips stay on the bench; no big low-back arch.

mistake.what: Low back arching away from the pad (hips pushing up) to press the bar.
mistake.why: Boostcamp names excessive low-back arching both as a form fault and as an injury risk; how often it happens is not measured in any source read.

tells.text: Hips and shoulders stay on pad

grip.type: Closed grip, palms forward (c4); thumbs wrapped (inherited, parent c4).
grip.handContact: Bar in the base of the palm (inherited, parent c5).

setup.step: Set the back pad to about 30 degrees and set the safety catches.
Sit back with head, shoulders and hips on the pad, feet flat.
Grip slightly wider than shoulders, wrists straight.
With a spotter, lift the bar out to straight arms above your shoulders.

posture.point: Head, shoulders and hips on the pad.
Elbows about 45-75 degrees from the torso, not flared.
Bar to the upper chest, never the neck.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Arching the low back off the pad to finish a rep.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep your back on the pad; build up to heavier weights gradually.
Keep them about 45-75 degrees from your body.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Bouncing the bar off the chest.

rows.where: Upper chest and front of the shoulders
Mostly the front of the shoulders, little in the chest
rows.means: Usually the bench is set too steep.
rows.fix: Lower the back pad toward 30 degrees.

rows.where: Pain in the shoulder or chest
rows.means: Usually a warning sign; shoulder injuries are common in lifting.

risks.risk: Bar over the face and neck: the upper-chest touch point is closest to the neck; wrap the thumbs and use a spotter or safety catches.
Weights dropping on the lifter is the most common weight-room injury mechanism.
Shoulder injuries are common in lifting and linked to poor technique; flared elbows strain the shoulder.

zooms.right: Bar in the base of the palm, thumb wrapped, wrist straight.
zooms.wrong: Bar high toward the fingers, wrist bent back.

zooms.right: Head, shoulders and hips on the pad.
zooms.wrong: Low back arched off the pad, hips pushing up.
